title: RPLidar obstacle avoidance on PX4 and ArduPilot: the complete build log
intro: Everything about the lidar project in one place: hardware, ArduPilot setup, the new PX4 driver and its tests, the PX4 patches, the QGroundControl radar, the desktop app, two flight controllers, and what comes next. Last updated 14 November 2026.

images.caption: Cube Orange Plus bench test with the lidar and the radar in QGroundControl.

sections: The goal

Give a multirotor 360 degree obstacle awareness from a Slamtec RPLidar A2M12 wired straight to the flight controller, with no companion computer, on both ArduPilot and PX4, and make the scan visible to the pilot. Two flight controllers are used: a Holybro Pixhawk 6X and a CubePilot Cube Orange Plus. This page is the single, running record of the work and is updated after every step until the flight tests.

Status today: the lidar works on both boards on the bench, under PX4 with a new driver and under ArduPilot with its native support. Nothing has flown yet.
The hardware

The RPLidar A2M12 is a 360 degree laser scanner (0.2 to 12 m) with a 3.3 V UART at 256000 baud. Its connector has five wires: red 5 V, yellow TX, green RX, black ground and blue MOTOCTL. It needs 4.9 to 5.2 V, about 450 to 600 mA when running and up to 1.5 A at start-up. Its front (0 degrees) is the side opposite the cable, and angles increase clockwise seen from above.

Wiring to TELEM2 (JST-GH, pin 1 is 5 V): yellow (lidar TX) to pin 3 (RX), green (lidar RX) to pin 2 (TX), black to pin 6 (ground). For the bench, red went to TELEM2 pin 1 and blue to TELEM1 pin 1. For flight, red and blue move to a separate 5 V BEC of 3 A or more, with its ground shared.

The flight controller first looked like a Pixhawk 6C, but the version command reported PX4_FMU_V6X and board id 53, so every firmware here targets the Pixhawk 6X.
Day one on ArduPilot: proving the wiring and the sensor

ArduPilot supports RPLidar natively, so it came first: if the lidar works there, the wiring and the sensor are proven before writing any code. I flashed ArduCopter 4.7.2 and set SERIAL2_PROTOCOL 11 (lidar), SERIAL2_BAUD 256, BRD_SER2_RTSCTS 0 (no flow control), PRX1_TYPE 5 (RPLidar), PRX1_ORIENT 0 and simple avoidance with AVOID_ENABLE 7, AVOID_BEHAVE 1, AVOID_MARGIN 2 and AVOID_DIST_MAX 5.

First trap: ArduPilot found the lidar and read its model (A2M12, hardware 6, firmware 1.32) but no distances came. The motor was not spinning. MOTOCTL has an internal pull-down, so the blue wire must be held at 3 to 5 V, otherwise the motor stays off while the sensor still answers commands. Tying blue to 5 V fixed it.

The scan was then confirmed in three tools: a small terminal viewer, QGroundControl's MAVLink Inspector and Mission Planner's proximity view. Left, right and back matched the room, and the front showed the laptop at 0.33 m.

Second finding: powered from the Pixhawk's own 5 V rail over USB, the supply measured 4.2 to 4.4 V, below the lidar's 4.9 V minimum. Fine for the bench, not for flight. In ArduPilot, Loiter stops at AVOID_MARGIN, AltHold only leans away, and Auto or RTL would need path planning (OA_TYPE), which is not set up.

sections.caption: Day one: Mission Planner's proximity view with the lidar on ArduCopter 4.7.2. The short arc in front is the laptop.

sections: Why PX4 needed a new driver

No PX4 release up to v1.17.0 has an RPLidar driver. PX4's Collision Prevention reads a uORB topic called obstacle_distance: 72 sectors of 5 degrees in the vehicle frame. Without a companion computer, nothing publishes it from a 360 degree serial lidar. Collision Prevention also only acts in Position mode and needs CP_DIST above 0 and MPC_POS_MODE set to acceleration based (4).
The PX4 driver

The driver (rplidar, modelled on PX4's LightWare SF45 driver) runs on a 5 ms work queue and talks the RPLidar legacy scan protocol. A state machine sends STOP, waits 100 ms, asks GET_HEALTH (resetting the sensor if it reports an error), reads GET_INFO, starts SCAN and then decodes 5-byte samples: quality, start flag, angle and distance. It needs two valid samples in a row to lock onto the stream and restarts the sensor after 1 s without data.

Each revolution, it keeps the closest return in every 5 degree sector and publishes one obstacle_distance message in the vehicle frame (FRD), projected onto the horizontal plane using the vehicle attitude. Sectors swept with no return are reported as free, sectors never sampled as unknown. Returns closer than the minimum distance are ignored, which also hides parts of the frame.

Parameters: SENS_RPLIDAR_CFG picks the port (102 = TELEM 2), RPL_BAUD (256000 for the A2M12), RPL_YAW_OFF (direction the lidar's front points, degrees clockwise from the nose), RPL_ORIENT_CFG (0 upright, 1 upside down), RPL_MIN_DIST (0.2 m) and RPL_MAX_DIST (12 m). The command rplidar status shows the port, state, model, health, scan rate, samples per turn, bytes sent and received, the last bytes received, and the error and resync counters. The byte counters were added during the investigation below.
Testing the driver before any hardware

A host test bench compiles the real driver with PX4's own warning flags against small stand-ins for PX4, then runs it against a simulated lidar in ten scenarios: normal scanning, motor off, corrupted bytes, a health error and reset, upside-down mounting, yaw offset, no sensor connected, split serial reads, 30 degree pitch and a slow 5 Hz scan. It passes with clang on Windows and g++ on Ubuntu.

The corrupted-bytes scenario found a real bug: random bytes could look like a new revolution and cause half-filled messages (18 per second instead of 10). A start flag arriving less than 40 ms after the previous one is now ignored.
Building the firmware

Building PX4 v1.17.0 for the Pixhawk 6X with the driver failed on flash size: 20.9 KB over, although the driver itself is only 4.4 KB. The standard target was already near full with that compiler. PX4's official multicopter variant drops fixed-wing and VTOL code and fits at 97 percent, the right variant for a quadcopter anyway.

I also built ArduPilot's simulation-on-hardware firmware for the 6X. It works as a bench simulator, but its proximity library is compiled out and the simulated lidar exists only in desktop simulation, so it cannot show or test the lidar. It is set aside; avoidance will be tested in software-in-the-loop simulation.
First run on PX4: the lidar that would not answer

Flashed onto the 6X, the driver started by itself on TELEM2 (/dev/ttyS4) at 256000 baud, sent its commands and received nothing, with the motor spinning. The new byte counters showed bytes sent and zero received. Zero, not garbage, meant nothing reached the receive pin at all, so it was not a parsing or baud-rate problem.

I checked every software layer against the ArduPilot setup that had worked: same UART5 and pins (PC12 and PD2), the 256000 baud passed straight through NuttX, flow control off, no inversion, the right clock, nothing else on the port, and a 4.6 V supply. On paper PX4 was correct.

An A/B test with the known-good firmware settled it. With ArduCopter back on the board and the wiring untouched, the lidar was silent there too, until the lidar alone was power-cycled. The lidar had locked up, and rebooting the flight controller never helped because the lidar kept its power.

Starting the driver by hand a minute after boot still found a frozen lidar, so the driver's commands were not to blame. The cause was in PX4's board code: the 6X configures its 5 V peripheral rail switch (PG4) to off in its early start-up and turns it on later, so every PX4 cold start gives the TELEM ports a short power cut in the middle of the lidar's own start-up. ArduPilot keeps that rail on.
The fix: keep the 5 V rail on at boot

A two-line board patch makes the rail start on, as ArduPilot does. With it, the lidar streamed on the first try after four out of four full power-offs, with no restarts and no errors. The patch lives in the project repository and is applied by the install script.

sections.caption: Pixhawk 6X bench test with the lidar and an early version of the desktop radar.

sections: Getting the scan to QGroundControl

Stock PX4 only sends OBSTACLE_DISTANCE to the ground station while Collision Prevention is running, which needs Position mode and GPS. A small MAVLink patch sends the driver's raw scan whenever Collision Prevention is idle (and gives Collision Prevention's own data priority when it runs), and adds the message to the USB link at 10 Hz. QGroundControl's MAVLink Inspector then showed OBSTACLE_DISTANCE at about 10 Hz with no commands typed.
A lidar radar inside QGroundControl

QGroundControl draws only a single-colour ring. To get a proper radar without rebuilding QGroundControl, I used the fact that it loads its Fly view instrument from a file named in its settings and accepts a local file there. The radar is a QML instrument loaded that way, with QGroundControl's own attitude and compass instrument kept below it.

What it shows: the front is up and matches the flight controller's arrow. Obstacles are red inside CP_DIST (read live from the vehicle, 2 m if missing), yellow up to twice that and green beyond. It shows the closest distance on each side (F, R, B, L), the closest overall, a north marker from the vehicle heading, the vehicle icon from the reported vehicle type (quad, hexa, octo, tri, helicopter, plane, VTOL, rover, boat), my name, and a NO LIDAR DATA warning when the scan stops for 1 s.

How it is used: it sits above the attitude instrument at the same width. Drag it anywhere and double-click to put it back. The mouse wheel or the minus and plus buttons change the range (1.5, 3, 6 or 12 m). Ctrl with the wheel, or the corner grip, changes its size, and the full-screen button fills the Fly view (close it with the cross or by clicking the dark background). QGroundControl remembers position, range and size. It only shows on the Fly view.

sections.caption: The radar instrument above QGroundControl's attitude indicator, with QGroundControl's own obstacle ring on the video panel.
Full-screen radar with live data: front matches the flight controller's arrow, red inside the stopping distance.

sections: QGroundControl settings changed

All changes are in QGroundControl's settings file, edited with QGroundControl closed. instrumentQmlFile2 points the Fly view instrument at the radar file. showObstacleDistanceOverlay turns on QGroundControl's own obstacle ring (around the drone on the map once it has GPS, and over the video panel). The video source is set to RTSP at the SIYI A8 mini's default address through the SIYI air unit; this is not tested with the camera yet. MainFlyWindowIsMap chooses whether the map or the video fills the Fly view; clicking the small window swaps them.

forwardMavlink was turned on so the desktop radar could run next to QGroundControl, then turned back off because QGroundControl shows a UDP link error whenever nothing listens. Reverting to QGroundControl's normal instrument is one line in the same file, or a right-click on the instrument.
A desktop radar app

A Python app, started by double-clicking a launcher, finds the flight controller's USB port by itself (Holybro, CubePilot, ArduPilot and PX4 USB ids) or listens to QGroundControl's forwarding. It shows the vehicle, mode and armed state, FRONT, RIGHT, BACK and LEFT distance cards, the same colours, vehicle icon and north marker, parking-sensor beeps that speed up inside CP_DIST, a keep-on-top switch, zoom and a no-data warning. On PX4 firmware without the MAVLink patch it reads the scan through PX4's shell instead.

sections.caption: Desktop radar app connected to the Cube Orange Plus over USB.

sections: The second flight controller: Cube Orange Plus

Before the change, the Cube ran ArduCopter 4.7.1 and its full parameter set was saved. Its PX4 board code switches the 5 V peripheral rail (PA8) the same way as the 6X, so it received the same kind of patch. The PX4 build for the Cube is the default variant and uses 99.4 percent of flash, so little room is left. On the Cube, TELEM2 is /dev/ttyS1. After setting the quad X airframe, the lidar port, MAV_1_CONFIG 0 and CP_DIST 2, the lidar streamed at about 22 Hz with no errors, including after a cold start.

Limits to keep in mind: the Cube passed one cold start so far, not four, and it was never tested without the rail patch, so whether it would freeze without it is unknown. Its 5 V rail on USB is even lower, 4.14 V, so the BEC is required on both boards.
Pixhawk 6X and Cube Orange Plus side by side

Both run PX4 v1.17.0 with the same driver, the same patches and the same displays. Pixhawk 6X: multicopter build, 97.0 percent flash, lidar on /dev/ttyS4, about 20 Hz and 184 samples per turn, 4 of 4 cold starts, 0 errors, 4.2 to 4.6 V on USB, also tested on ArduCopter 4.7.2. Cube Orange Plus: default build, 99.4 percent flash, lidar on /dev/ttyS1, about 22 Hz and 183 samples per turn, 1 cold start, 0 errors, 4.14 V on USB, not tested with the lidar on ArduPilot. The project page has the full table.
Mounting the lidar on the drone

Easiest: mount it level and right side up with its front (opposite the cable) toward the drone's nose, so RPL_YAW_OFF stays 0. Turned mounts are corrected with RPL_YAW_OFF (90 if it points right, 180 if the cable points forward, 270 if it points left), and an upside-down mount with RPL_ORIENT_CFG 1. On ArduPilot the same settings are PRX1_YAW_CORR and PRX1_ORIENT. Mount it high enough that props and the GPS mast do not block the beam. After mounting, a hand in front of the drone must lower the FRONT distance; if another side reacts, the offset is wrong.
What is published

Everything is open source on GitHub: the PX4 driver and its tests, the three PX4 patches, the QGroundControl radar, the desktop app, ArduPilot parameters, built firmware for both boards and Ubuntu build scripts. Link: github.com/HRAFRH/rplidar-obstacle-avoidance
What comes next

1. Fit the BEC for the lidar and confirm the supply is about 5 V.

2. Mount the lidar on the drone and check directions by hand.

3. Finish the flight setup (radio, flight modes, failsafes).

4. Software-in-the-loop simulation with a simulated RPLidar to tune stopping distance and behaviour.

5. Test Collision Prevention outdoors in Position mode, props off first, then the first flights.

6. Test the SIYI A8 video with the obstacle ring over the camera picture.

This page will be updated with each of these steps.

title: Reading pitch tracking and vibration on an FPV quadcopter
intro: What an FPV flight log can tell you before changing the tune.
sections: Compare the command with the response
I began with commanded and measured pitch. The actual response broadly followed the command, but the overshoot and oscillation gave me a reason to look at the tune and the vibration data together.
Use the spectrum to guide the next check

The FFT highlighted several bands to investigate. I treated motor-related vibration and possible frame resonance as different candidates and documented how to check the proposed filtering on this specific airframe.
Record what still needs a test
The report excerpts show the diagnosis and recommendations. The next step is to compare fresh logs after a controlled change, using the same tracking and vibration measurements.

title: Before the field: building a useful aircraft simulation
intro: Custom models, autopilot connections and the checks I can repeat before a real flight.
sections: Start with the aircraft I intend to fly

I simulate many of my aircraft before field testing. The purpose is practical: understand how the components and control interfaces fit together, explore behaviour, and check flight modes, parameters and mission workflows in a repeatable environment.
Go beyond a pre-built model

For the Cobra VTOL, I converted the aircraft files into a custom Gazebo model and integrated it with PX4 and ArduPilot. That lets the simulation work follow the aircraft configuration I am developing, rather than treating a generic simulator vehicle as an exact representation of the build.
Make each screenshot explain one thing

The examples here show different parts of the work: a Skywalker X8 QuadPlane model, a PX4 multirotor in a wooded world, RC and servo-channel displays, and model axes beside mission planning. One QuadPlane screenshot also preserves a command warning. It records troubleshooting, not an automatically successful test.
Take a clearer question to the field

Simulation helps me prepare configurations and decide what I need to observe during physical testing. I then use real flight tests and recorded behaviour to continue the work. A custom model is useful preparation, not a guarantee that every physical effect has been reproduced.

title: Cobra VTOL: connecting the workshop build to a custom model
intro: Keeping the physical aircraft and its simulation in the same development workflow.
sections: Build the physical interfaces
The Cobra workshop photographs show the airframe and lift-propulsion layout during assembly and integration. I worked on the aircraft as a connected structure, propulsion and avionics system.
Bring that configuration into Gazebo

I also converted the Cobra aircraft files into a custom Gazebo model and connected it to PX4 and ArduPilot. The objective was to explore the configuration and prepare useful checks before field testing.
Keep the images specific

These are Cobra assembly photographs. The separate simulation entry shows its own identified aircraft and software screenshots. A matching view of the custom Cobra simulator model can extend this story when it is available.

title: The Ranger held level, but kept turning right
intro: Working through a fixed-wing yaw problem with the client, one configuration check at a time.
sections: Start with the behaviour

The Volantex Ranger was a pusher fixed wing running INAV. The client reported that it held level in stabilised modes but continued yawing to the right, with left rudder needed to counter the turn. Keeping the wings level had not solved the heading problem.
Separate the possible causes

I reviewed the configuration rather than treating every turn as a PID problem. The report identifies board-alignment offsets, the magnetometer configuration and strong yaw feed-forward as points to investigate. Rudder direction, control authority and the pusher thrust line were also part of the diagnosis. These were hypotheses to test, not five independently proven faults.
Make the next test useful

I prepared an ordered set of checks so the client could isolate one influence at a time. A separate Blackbox guide explained how to prepare the recorder and retrieve the next log. The two documents are visible below, alongside the reasoning they supported. Their settings belong to this aircraft and are not a universal fixed-wing configuration.
Keep the outcome tied to the evidence

I helped the client resolve the yaw issue. The documents shown here preserve the investigation and support work; they do not include a final post-fix flight log. Matching client photographs and flight recordings will be added when available, so another aircraft is not used as a substitute.

title: From a drone that would not fly to a payload delivery
intro: Arabic coaching, remote commissioning and a 5 kg delivery mission, one practical step at a time.
sections: Start with the person as well as the aircraft

The client had bought a heavy-lift drone, but it was not flying. He was new to drones and unfamiliar with the flight modes and operating workflow. My role was to work through the aircraft with him while teaching the process from the beginning, in Arabic, so the instructions were useful to the person carrying out the work.
Make remote work practical

Everything was done through calls and screen sharing. I reviewed the build, prepared the parameters and guided him through calibration and setup on the computer connected to the aircraft. The system used a CUAV X7+ flight controller and a SIYI transmission system specified for up to 30 km; that product rating is separate from the range demonstrated by this mission.
Build confidence before adding a mission

I made the first steps easier by using Loiter mode for more stable position-holding practice. We worked through what each mode did and how to operate the aircraft before progressing to a planned mission. The difficulty was not simply changing parameters: the client needed a sequence he could understand, repeat and use in the field.
Prepare the power system and the release

Support included the batteries and charger, not only the flight controller. I explained the charging workflow for the mission setup, which used a reported 12S 40,000 mAh LiPo configuration. We also configured the servo-operated gripper and its mission action for the 5 kg bag of rice. The component close-ups below show different stages and battery packs from the project.
Plan the delivery, then review what happened

Once he was comfortable with the aircraft, I taught him how to prepare the mission. The client completed the payload drop and the drone returned successfully. The matching log review records 20.25 km of total out-and-return travel and a 10.11 km maximum displacement. This is roughly a 10 km outbound mission, not a 20 km one-way delivery.
Use the difficulties to improve the next test

The work involved explaining unfamiliar modes, checking the build remotely, guiding calibration and connecting the release mechanism to the mission. The log review also records a radio-failsafe transition to RTL, vibration and accelerometer clipping, and current readings that need calibration before they can support energy estimates. I keep those findings in the engineering record alongside the successful delivery outcome.
What the project taught me

A useful remote handover has to work for the person on site. In this case, teaching in Arabic, reviewing the screen together and progressing from setup to Loiter practice and then mission preparation turned the support into a practical operating workflow. The photographs and recordings preserve those stages; matching mission evidence is shown separately in the report.

title: Printing and integrating a twin-pusher fixed-wing aircraft
intro: Tornado V2 airframe fabrication, Pixhawk 6C integration and the checks behind field testing.
sections: Start with the airframe and its interfaces

For these builds I used the Titan Dynamics Tornado V2 airframe design. My work covered printing and assembly, propulsion and avionics integration, configuration and testing. The two pusher motors and conventional tail distinguish this aircraft from the four-lift-motor QuadPlanes elsewhere in the portfolio.
Balance printing weight with build practicality

I printed the shown airframe builds in ABS using 3% infill and one perimeter, balancing airframe weight with practical rigidity for assembly and handling. The photographs follow the work from wing and fuselage sections on the printer to laid-out parts and assembled aircraft.
Connect propulsion, surfaces and avionics

The build paired Pixhawk 6C with ArduPlane 4.6.3 and twin-pusher propulsion. I integrated navigation, power and onboard wiring, and worked through control-surface directions, stabilization response and differential-thrust checks. Configuration and log review helped connect each test to the next integration step.
Keep the public evidence useful

The open-fuselage views show the hardware integration, while the assembled aircraft images show the finished build stages. The log-review visual has its satellite map and identifying information removed. It provides illustrative review context, not exact flight-path or performance data.

title: Building a 2.2 m QuadPlane as one connected system
intro: Lift propulsion, cruise propulsion and avionics had to work together before field testing.
sections: The challenge: two flight regimes, one aircraft

The Cube Orange QuadPlane combined four lift motors with separate forward propulsion. That made the integration broader than mounting a flight controller. Airframe assembly, power distribution, control electronics and radio links all had to fit into one testable aircraft.
Working through the integration sequence

I integrated the structural components, propulsion, autopilot electronics, GNSS, RC and telemetry, then worked through sensor calibration and configuration. ArduPilot and PX4 workflows formed part of the development work. Bench checks established a baseline before control tuning, transition work and mission testing in the field.
The result and the next evidence

The delivered work included an assembled aircraft and an iterative sequence of configuration and field tests. Existing photographs show the fuselage integration, bench setup and aircraft in the field. I keep those stages visible because they explain the engineering behind the aircraft without turning a photograph into a performance claim.

title: From printed structures to a tiltrotor test platform
intro: A V-tail tricopter VTOL brought mechanical assembly and flight-control configuration into the same development loop.
sections: The challenge: connect the moving mechanisms

A tiltrotor adds a mechanical interface to the control problem. The structure, propulsion units, servos and sensors have to work as a coordinated system. My work covered printed components and assembly as well as the electronics and autopilot setup.
Use a matching test configuration

I integrated the propulsion, servos and sensors and worked with Pixhawk-family and SpeedyBee ArduPilot configurations. A matching tricopter setup helped investigate settings before wider VTOL testing. This kept configuration work tied to the actual propulsion arrangement rather than treating the aircraft as a generic multirotor.
What reached testing

The project record includes assembly, hovering and maiden-test material, alongside mission-planning and configuration work. The photographs and system overview show the development stages. They describe a working development effort, with test scope kept separate from any claim of production qualification.

title: Giving a Micro Talon vertical takeoff capability
intro: The conversion linked new lift hardware to the fixed-wing aircraft's existing cruise role.
sections: The challenge: add lift without losing the aircraft

Converting a fixed-wing airframe into a QuadPlane changes its mechanical and electrical interfaces. Four lift motors need mounting, power and control, while forward propulsion and the original flight surfaces remain part of the aircraft.
Build, configure and check the handoff

I produced mounting parts, integrated the lift propulsion and electronics, and configured the SpeedyBee F405 WING Mini with ArduPlane. Calibration, hover modes, transition parameters and mission setup were part of the same integration sequence.
The recorded result

The project includes a physical VTOL conversion and a documented flight-test sequence, including an initial QStabilize takeoff and landing. That is the validation I show. Wider transition reliability is a separate question and is not inferred from a single successful takeoff.

title: Building a 10-inch FPV aircraft for assisted flight and missions
intro: Propulsion, power, flight controls and failsafes were developed as a complete aircraft.
sections: The challenge: go beyond a frame and motors

The 6S quadcopter needed to support manual handling, assisted flight and waypoint missions. The component choices and electrical integration therefore had to serve both the aircraft's propulsion demands and its autopilot functions.
Connect hardware to behaviour

I selected propulsion and power components, integrated Pixhawk 6X and sensors, and completed wiring and calibration. I then worked on flight modes, mission setup, failsafes and PID tuning. This joined the bench integration to the behaviour that would be checked in the field.
What was tested

The documented work includes assisted-flight and mission testing, plus approximately 2 kg payload testing for this development configuration. Bench and field images show the aircraft at different stages. Those checks belong to this build and are not a payload guarantee for every 10-inch aircraft.

title: Making a compact INAV FPV build ready for flight
intro: A 3-inch platform connected power, radio control and firmware setup in a small airframe.
sections: The challenge: small aircraft still need full integration

Compact FPV aircraft leave little room for poor component placement or unclear wiring. This project brought together a 4S power system, flight-control electronics and ExpressLRS radio control within a small frame.
Bring the interfaces into one setup

I worked through the wiring, firmware configuration and control setup, including Angle and Horizon mode tuning. The objective was a coherent stabilized FPV configuration, with radio and flight-control behaviour checked together.
The delivered scope

The project record includes the build, documented wiring and flight-validation work for stabilized FPV flying. Its role is different from the autonomous mission platforms elsewhere in the portfolio. Keeping it separate makes the compact-aircraft integration work easier to see.

title: Establishing an S500 autopilot and sensor baseline
intro: A sensor-equipped quadcopter connected propulsion, navigation and telemetry before stability checks.
sections: The challenge: make the integration observable
A development aircraft needs more than a powered flight controller. GNSS, telemetry and calibrated sensors are part of understanding what the vehicle is doing and preparing useful tests.
Build the baseline

I integrated Pixhawk 6X, GNSS, telemetry and propulsion interfaces on the S500, completed calibration and parameter setup, and worked on flight-stability checks. The focus was to bring these elements into one configured development platform.
What the project shows

The delivered work is the S500 hardware integration, sensor calibration and development testing. The current image documents the avionics setup. Additional photographs can extend the build record without changing the scope of the work already described.

title: Finding where a LiDAR proximity pipeline was delayed
intro: Sensor output, autopilot input and the ground-station display needed to be examined separately.
sections: The challenge: a delayed display is not a diagnosis

The integration connected a Unitree L2 LiDAR pipeline to ArduPilot through companion computing. Proximity information appeared delayed, but the visible symptom alone could not establish whether the delay came from sensing, transport, autopilot input or display rendering.
Trace the data path

I reviewed the ROS 2 and MAVROS path into MAVLink OBSTACLE_DISTANCE, together with serial mapping and proximity settings. I separated sensor-to-autopilot latency from ground-station rendering and proposed ground checks to examine the interfaces and timing.
An actionable investigation

The output was an integration findings report with validation steps. It narrowed the questions for the next checks instead of treating an unverified tuning change as a complete solution. The public report excerpts show the approach; universal obstacle-avoidance performance is not claimed.

title: Commissioning the ground-drive stage of a hybrid aircraft
intro: The wheeled-aircraft project required its own motor-control and safety baseline.
sections: The challenge: separate the two operating modes

An aircraft that can drive on wheels brings different control paths into one platform. This engagement focused on the ground unit before the later flight-and-drive merge. It is a separate project from the drone landing on a rover.
Make ground commands explicit

I integrated the CUAV X7+ ArduRover baseline, dual VESC motor paths, skid-steer mixing and RC safety gating. The work connected the operator commands and autopilot configuration to the wheel-drive interfaces.
The delivered milestone

I documented the ground-control behaviour, setup and next integration steps in a commissioning report. The ground milestone is the completed delivery shown here. Combining wheel operation with flight was a later stage, so I do not present it as a finished hybrid-flight result.

title: Connecting perception to a usable vehicle payload
intro: Detection, camera control and video transport belong to the same integration problem.
sections: The challenge: make the output useful to the vehicle and operator

A detection model by itself is not a complete payload. The camera stream, companion computer, tracking workflow and gimbal or platform interface all have to connect. My work covered those interfaces across embedded vehicle applications.
Join compute, camera and transport

I integrated Jetson and Raspberry Pi companion computing, YOLOv8 and ByteTrack workflows, and camera or gimbal interfaces with RTSP and GStreamer video transport. On the USV work, Jetson Nano and an A8C gimbal connected first-person video and AI-detection workflows with operator visibility.
The delivered work

The contribution was integration of perception, video and platform interfaces. The project is presented as an embedded payload workflow rather than an unsupported accuracy or autonomy claim. Its supporting images provide the hardware context, with room for more application-specific material.
